title: Late-night uncertainty memo: Omar Ghosh (runtime candidate)
body:
Context:
- Interview loop today (system-design + live-coding + two behavioral threads). Omar has strong background on systems (ex-ML infra at a mid-size cloud provider) but there were recurring hesitation points when we drilled into tradeoffs for production inference (latency SLOs vs aggressive batching, cache eviction causes).

Quick read (TL;DR):
- Strengths: solid mental model for GPU utilization, clear familiarity with kernel/quantization tradeoffs, calm under pressure.
- Concerns: fuzzy on operational fallback policies and concrete rollout steps; gave plausible but vague answers to KV cache invalidation in multi-tenant settings. 2–3 small clarifying questions could move him into a confident hire.

Notes by segment:
1) System design (45m)
- Prompt: design a multi-tenant inference pool that supports two model sizes and provides tail-latency SLO of 95th < 150ms for tail requests while allowing cost-optimized batching for non-interactive workloads.
- What went well: outlined separation of latency-critical and throughput buckets, proposed tagging requests with SLO-class and having separate routing pools. Proposed cache (prefix) hit boosting and hinted at KV cache warmup during rollouts.
- Wobbles: when asked how to handle cold-starts across pinned model versions and autoscaler decisions, his answer stayed high level ("we could pre-warm" / "increase reserved slots") without concrete metrics or heuristics (e.g., what to pre-warm, how long to keep warm, cost math).
- Follow-ups to ask in a second pass: what metrics would you track to decide when to demote a model variant from latency pool to throughput pool? How would you instrument to detect cache fragmentation across tenants?

2) Live coding (30m)
- Task: implement a tiny LRU-style TTL cache wrapper for KV-lookup with eviction callback to persist misses. (Whiteboard -> pair in editor)
- What went well: produced working prototype quickly, tests for basic correctness, talked through complexity analysis (O(1) for core ops). Implementation idiomatic in Python, good naming, caught off-by-one edge when I seeded the cache.
- Wobbles: skipped discussion about thread-safety under high concurrency (we pushed him to talk about locking/sharding), suggested a coarse-grain lock then reverted to optimistic plan. Code would need explicit concurrency plan for C++/Rust runtime but he did not concretely propose sharded locks or lockless structures.

3) Behavioral / culture (20m)
- Examples of working across product/CS: gave at least two good stories where he negotiated rollback windows and SLA grace periods with product managers. Emphasized owning customer communication during incidents.
- Collaboration signals: likes codewalks, open to pairing, references specific maintainer feedback loops he ran.

Signal map (rough):
- Tech depth (systems): 7/10 — strong conceptual knowledge, pragmatic.
- Production ops instincts: 5.5/10 — has the right instincts but lacks concrete playbook answers for rollouts and fallbacks in complex multi-tenant runtimes.
- Coding / implementation: 8/10 — clean, test-first, moves fast.
- Culture fit for team: 7/10 — assertive but collaborative.
- My gut hire confidence: 6/10 (leans hire with a focused follow-up to close ops gaps).

Concrete concerns (enumerated):
- Missing: explicit rollout/incremental rollout blueprint (canary %s, ramp triggers, fail-open vs fail-closed rules).
- Missing: exact heuristics for when to evict cache entries across tenants that share prefixes — risk of cross-tenant pollution/latency spikes.
- Concurrency plan for production runtime: coarse answers; needs to articulate lock-sharding, epoch-based reclamation, or lockless queue designs for hot-path KV cache ops.

Positive signals (enumerated):
- Reads perf counters well; knows what counters to query on GPU utilization and KV cache hit/miss latency.
- Empathy for product/customer: concrete stories showing he kept customers informed during degraded performance.
- Quick prototyping ability: wrote a clean, testable cache wrapper in under 30m.

Suggested closure plan (what I'd like to see before offering or passing to manager):
1) Short follow-up assignment (take-home, 2–4 hours): craft a one-page "canary + rollback" runbook for a model variant rollout in a multi-tenant environment. Must include: metrics to monitor, exact ramp percentages/timing, rollback triggers, and a short cost estimate for pre-warm capacity.
2) Optional technical phone: 20m focused on concurrency for hot-path KV cache — ask for sketch of sharding strategy and memory reclamation plan (concrete diagrams encouraged).
3) Ask references for specific incident where they had to change behavior of runtime under load — did they lead the decision and what were the signals?

Interviewer's suggested scorecard (fields to pass along):
- System design: 6/10 (good separation of concerns, weaker on concrete rollout/metrics)
- Implementation: 8/10
- Ops/runbook: 5/10
- Cross-team communication: 7/10
- Recommend next step: follow-up assignment + targeted phone call

Short suggested wording for the hiring panel (for quick paste):
- "Omar showed solid runtime and systems instincts and is a very capable implementer. He hesitated on concrete rollout/eviction heuristics — recommend a short take-home to evaluate how he operationalizes rollback and cache strategies; if that looks good, move to manager interview."

Follow-up prompts/questions to bring into the take-home (so the take-home is tightly scoped):
- "We have two model variants: small-v1 (optimized, quantized) and large-v2 (higher quality). Explain a rollout plan to expose 10% of customers to large-v2 with minimal risk to latency SLO. Include rollout buckets, pre-warm costs, cache-warmup heuristics, and explicit rollback criteria."
- "Design a strategy to ensure tenant boundaries are respected in prefix KV caching to avoid cross-tenant pollution while maintaining high cache hit rates. Provide metric triggers for when to isolate a tenant's cache."

Open questions / things I want to check quickly with ref checks:
- Did Omar own any autoscaling or pre-warm logic in previous role? If yes, what were the rules he used?
- Has he shipped operational runbooks that were used during incidents (and did changes reduce incident time-to-recover)?

Final micro-note (tone / hiring rationale):
- I would hire him if the follow-up take-home demonstrates concrete, measurable plans for rollouts and cache management. He ticks most boxes for the role but needs to move from "good instincts" to "repeatable playbook".

Quick TODO for panel handoff:
- Attach his coding snippet (PR link above) and ask for a 20m manager session focused on incident ownership and production concurrency.
- If manager also okay, add him to a short-window offer contingent on passing the take-home within 5 business days.

End of memo.

(Notes-to-self: keep the follow-up assignment narrow — avoid long take-homes; the goal is to see operational specificity, not building infrastructure.)
